title: What to watch during training camp | Bears Weekly
text: Welcome in [music] to Bears Weekly, a Chicago Bears Network production. Bears Weekly [music] is brought to you by Advocate Health Care, Athletico Physical Therapy, CDW, Connie's Pizza, and Miller Lite. Here are your [music] hosts, Jeff Joniak, aka the Mayor of Bearsville, and his sidekick Tom [music] the Surf Master Thayer. >> By this time next week, your Bears will be on the practice field gearing up for a significant season. Year two under Ben Johnson with high expectations and loads [music] of intrigue. We discuss tonight on Bears Weekly on the ESPN 1000 and the Chicago Bears Radio Network with Super Bowl winning Bears guard Tom Thayer and former Bears quarterback Jim Miller. I'm Jeff Joniak. Dan Berilly, Jordan Treadup, Katie Fox are producers in studio tonight. Kendra Smith, executive producer of the Bears Radio Network, is Eric Austrowski. Coming up in tonight's program, we hear from rookie safety Dylan Tevlin, linebacker Jack Sanborn back with the Bears, and second-year interior offensive lineman Luke Nieuwmann. Gentlemen, very excited. We talk about the excitement every every week leading up every day and some of the guys we're going to hear from tonight excite me including that safety Dylan Tevlin, Tom. He is going to become a cornerstone piece we hope for this Bears defense for now and in the future. >> Well, that's why they drafted him number one. You know, as we sat here a year ago, it was all about anticipation. Anticipation of Caleb, anticipation of Ben Johnson and his staff. This year, it's expectations. You talk about guys like Dylan or Caleb or Ben, everybody that we have at really high expectations for. >> Yeah, you know, a lot's going to be expected of Dylan. You know, when you get drafted nowadays in the first round, a lot of the expectation that Tom's talking about is you're expected to be an impactful player and you're going to be contributing for a very quickly. Um sounds like his biggest assignment is coming up with a handshake for all the DBs. So, that's just another thing on his plate uh that he's got to work on, but he knows he knows he's under a microscope. Everybody's watching him and I think he's he's ready for the challenge. I do. >> Guys, what what also peaks your curiosity as we move closer to camp? Tom, maybe something out of the ordinary because all the focus obviously is on the battles, but the tackle position, the competition on the defensive line, how that all turns out, the linebacker level, the health of the football team. What what else is on your mind? >> You know, a lot of it my eyes gravitate towards Kyle Monangai, Colston Loveland, and Luther Burden on the offensive side of the ball because last year they came into camp, but we didn't know where they were going to fit in, how they were going to fit in, or when they were going to fit in. And then by the fourth game, they all had their positions and Ben knew exactly what to expect out of them and what he could get out of them, and they were significant contributors from that point on. And then when I go to the defensive side of the ball, Jeff, I'm still super curious about Shamarr Turner because here's a guy that when you talk about a position that rotates seven or eight guys per game day active, he can make a whole position better. And if he comes in with the young, brash, explosive, quick-twitch fibers that we've seen him have when he is healthy, I'm really excited to see what Shamarr Turner can contribute because he's a guy that could burst onto the scenes just like Luther, Colston, and Kyle did last year on offense. >> Yeah, I think it's the second-year players or going into their second year, the jump that they're going to make. I agree with Tom. Turner, we don't know he's kind of an unknown. We know he's talented, but we didn't get to see him last year. So, what is the jump that he's going to have? You know, even though we haven't seen it. So, it's big for him. Caleb goes without question. Your quarterback is always going to be looked at. He's still very young in the process, but he's got a lot of areas of improvement we're looking for. We you've talked about the completion percentage, how he plays in the first and the third quarters rather than just finishing games. And just again, it's the rookies that contribute to this year. You know, I think uh they've got a good solid foundation that they built last year that they're looking to to build upon. And a lot of guys now are going to have to start to take ownership. I I think they they earned that last year. And and now they know that they're under a spotlight. And we'll see how they handle that pressure cuz there is a lot of expectation that Tom's talking about. You know, some of those second-year players were on the building at Halas Hall for the majority of the offseason. Guys like Cole Kmet, guys like Luther Burden, both getting stronger in the weight room. And I just went back and looked at some of their statistics from a year ago. Loveland wound up 107 targets with 90 catches and 906 uh yards. >> Six touchdowns. And that was including the playoffs. He had seven plays of 25-plus. In those final four games, including the two playoff games, guys, 48 targets. He had games of 94, 91, and 137. Uh so, we we know this is a wide receiver in a tight end body. It gives a lot of flexibility to Ben Johnson to uh incorporate not just him, but the other tight ends as well, Cole Kmet uh prominently. And we'll see about Sam Rauch this year, the fifth-round pick. Uh but also the impact of Burden, who had at least five targets a game over eight of his final nine games and really came on strong the second half of the season. Jim and Tom, uh looking at Loveland and Burden, can they emerge as impact players at a level that we see the direction started last year? Can they take it to that next level right now? >> You know, Jeff, one thing I want to say about Cole Kmet and Loveland is remember a couple weeks ago we were sitting across the table from Cole Kmet. And as he got up and he left the room, we both looked at each other and said, "Wow, this dude is yolked." I mean, you can see I think that's the same that we got to expect out of Cole Kmet and Loveland. Because last year, when he was rehabilitating a shoulder injury, you don't really have a chance to get underneath the weights, whether you're doing legs or bench presses or shoulder presses or whatever. So, I expect a bigger, stronger, more dominant Cole Kmet Loveland because of he's not rehabbing, he's working out. And so, I think that'll be a difference and I think that a guy like Luther Burden um he's comfortable inside the building. And I think when you create an atmosphere for these guys to become comfortable and confident and they like being there, I think that's when you get to continue to see the best out of them as they mature in an NFL body. >> I I think they're in a really good spot because, you know, everybody says, "Well, is you know, who's the true number one on the team?" You know, like I said, last year Rome Odunze was leading the Bears in receptions till he got hurt. And then, of course, Cole Kmet emerged as the as the leader in receptions. So, you know, you've got kind of two number ones there or they've shown that they can be the the leaders. I think Luther Burden showed times last year late in the season where he emerged where Ben Johnson, game planning-wise, he can go in and use all these guys as one. Hey, we're going to feature Luther Burden this week or we're going to feature uh Cole Kmet this week or we're going to feature Rome Odunze this week and we'll see about the young rookie and Zavian what he can do and and then, of course, the running backs. I think you've got a full menu, a buffet of guys that you can feature. And they've got to be unselfish, but if they do start to make plays, of course, they're going to earn that right to to get more opportunities and we'll see who really emerges as a true number one. And I know they're all going to be competing like hell to to be that guy. They really will be. >> All right, coming up next, we'll hear from Dylan Cole Kmet and the Bears rookie safety. This is ESPN 1000 and the Chicago Bears Radio Network. >> Welcome back to Bears Weekly, a Chicago Bears production on the flagship home of the Bears, [music] ESPN Chicago. >> Welcome back to ESPN 1000 and Bears radio network with Super Bowl winning Bears guard Tom Thayer. I'm Jeff Joniak. We got the first round pick Dylan at number 31. Is he feeling comfortable now in navy blue and orange? >> I'm glad I got it on. >> Yeah, it looks good. It looks good. So, are you are you a multiple handshake guy? Cuz I look at these young guys they get introduced or >> with like different people. >> Like Josh Allen from the Buffalo quarterback. I've never seen a guy have more individual handshakes. >> How do you remember? >> Like are you that guy or >> I'm not that guy. I like to make one for like the DBs. >> Right. >> a whole. So, I'll make one and then or like someone will make one and then we'll all just do it every time. >> Is that already started you think? >> Uh we got a little thing going. So, we'll see how it >> [laughter] >> Yeah, it's it is fascinating how that works, man. I think that's kind of sports today when you think even baseball now with you know when guys hit home runs they got a whole thing going on. But it's a it's a cool sign that camaraderie's brewing too, right? And and as how long it takes for chemistry between the safeties because it's as critical as anything on the defense to connect and from your experience just even in the college game, uh how do you bridge that gap? >> Just more just getting reps out there on the field and then also just getting to know the person too. Like if you get to know some like how they do things or how they operate and then when you get on the field it's like a lot of people are pretty similar. Um on and off the field and really just building that bond and so that you know that what kind of what they're thinking before you guys have to say anything. >> Up to this point do you find yourself doing more listening or asking more questions or a little of both? >> Uh more more listening still. >> Yeah. >> Um being around the whole team they're able to see both sides of the ball now like before OTA practices it was more just like just offense and just defense. But definitely learning from from E and and Kobe in the room and and asking them some questions, too. >> Do you become familiar with the way a receiver runs routes if you see him often enough? Cuz here you're going to be in a division, you're going to play each team a couple times, so you become a little bit more familiar with your divisional opponents. Do you take into account like route running, or is it all specifically assignment generated responsibility? >> No, you definitely get a feel for for route running, either scheme-wise or like the wide receiver individually or tight end. Talk about my experience back in college, like playing I mean playing the Big Ten, playing those teams over and over again, you kind of see a pattern of uh either how the schemes work or uh certain guys how they run run their routes. Like some people like to take like a bigger step right before they break, or they have like some of their favorite route combinations that they do. >> You know, I've I've been wanting to ask you this since the Bears drafted you, cuz we've all paid attention to your highlight films, we see the way you play football, the program that you came from. But I was always interested the track program at Oregon, it's as significant as there is in in college. When you talk about the 40 that you ran and what you expected, did you do anything with the track program there in terms of maybe learning how to run better, how to come out of the blocks, any straight line speed or experience, or was that something that you really didn't participate in? >> I didn't really do anything track-wise there. I know that um De'Anthony Thomas, he was a freshman last year when I was there, but he he did like some long jump event like for the track team. >> Uh this past uh like a month or two ago, but I didn't really do anything with them. I worked a lot with uh our football speed coach um Kyle Bolt. >> Is there anything specifically that again going back to the 40 that you ran, was there anything specifically that when you started getting ready for pro days, combines, and everything that you concentrated on to get ready to be the most explosive uh person you could be? >> Uh, for me, I had a good back end speed. Uh, so it was really just focusing on that, uh, that first 10. So, um, the huge thing about me is like I wanted to to stand up really quick. So, my main focus was staying low through that first, uh, 5-10 yards and driving like forward more than driving up. >> Right. Isn't it crazy so much attention is put on that and you'll never run it again? >> Mhm. >> Unless you want to. Right? They Nobody's going to time you anymore. >> This is your last time doing it. >> Yeah, it's not going to be an annual thing, but it that number now lives with you for the 15 years you might play in the National Football League, right? They're still going to know you were a 4-3 guy. It's just kind of funny to me all the time. When when you're going through this process now, it probably doesn't feel like it yet, but uh, you're there's no time off as a rookie, right? You had to get ready for the combine, you played a lot of games at Oregon, um, and then you're going to play a long season. Have you been told about just how the mental part of that you have to prepare for and try to conquer? >> Yeah, a lot of a lot of guys have brought that up. How long it's going to feel that you just from going uh, last season in college training and then getting through this season. Um, and a lot of them talk about the wall. >> The rookie wall, uh, hit about game 13, 12-13. But right now my mindset is probably just going to be take it week by week. >> Don't need to look too far ahead. >> I got to be honest with you and maybe because they were banged up a little bit in preseason, Colston Loveland and Luther Burden, I I don't think they hit the wall last year, right? I mean, we talked about that on the broadcast many times. Well, I think Maybe they did, but I don't know. I mean, they they plowed right through it. >> The game day excitement, the way they were winning games, I think it takes the wall away because you're so excited to get back at practice the next week because you just had one of the most exciting wins and this this team and this organization is going somewhere where it hasn't been in a long time with Ben and his staff. >> Yeah, I mean, from being on the field opposed from like being maybe in the locker room or or mentally, uh could be a few different things. So, they could have been just firing on the field, but still kind of feeling it a little on the other side. Uh I don't know exactly. Just saying, but they they could have been just great, too. >> Yeah. Are you Do you find yourself filled with excitement about what's coming? >> Mhm. Yeah, I mean, I'm I'm I'm extremely excited. Very excited for what's to come to to get back out there on the field, but I also know it's going to it's going to be a long process, like going through the rest of uh mini camp here, and then we got some time off, and then coming back for training camp and preseason. Like, it's going to be a very long journey. So, just taking it like day by day, like one step at a time. >> Yeah. Do you think the transfer from Purdue to Oregon has helped you prepare from going from Oregon to the Bears? And, you know, mentally, you know how to absorb change? >> Yeah. Cuz uh I mean, you're starting in a whole new environment when I was going to Oregon. Whole new environment, new scheme, new coaches, different part of the country. So, uh I feel like already making that jump, I know what works for me and what doesn't. And then, making the jump here, um again, has just made the transition like >> And you you know what the Midwest weather's like. So, you know, going out >> So, have you Have you I we just asked Kevin Bush this, and he went through it. He just got a big grin on his face about Ben's offense. The the different things they throw at a defense, and you guys are are learning this, you know, from three tight ends to whatever Whatever the case may be. That the responsibilities and what they are going to get you ready for is pretty significant. Is that playbook is insane? Have you already noticed some of that? >> Yes, I've noticed a lot of that. Um he definitely likes to to target some guys on the defense, and um draw some plays to get some uh the athletes on the offense the ball. Um but I feel like going against that will be extremely beneficial. Cuz like, if you're going against some of the best, it's just going to make you better. So, uh Uh, seeing that now and seeing it early on is just going to help us further down the >> The process of being a rookie, have you figured out where to live yet? Have you Are all those things taken care of? Do you have people taking care of that for you so you can focus on football or how's that going? >> Yeah, I have a I have a great team around me with my family and my agent agency. Um, definitely help me with all that stuff. Decided on a place to place to live and >> Um, just taking it >> So you can just >> Yeah, all [clears throat] ball ball. >> focus more and kind of like delegated a little bit. >> Exactly. >> Is there any Is there any relatable terminology from college to Ben or Dennis Allen's system or is it completely new and you got to, you know, reset the memory? There's some carryover and some not. And some of the schemes are a little pretty similar, but like say you get to cover four, like the progressions are a little different. Right. So some of that stuff might be a little different. >> Get ready for training camp. Are you going to be You got You got something already cooking [clears throat] for the the team meetings? Are you dancing? Are you singing? Are >> I mean, it's a pressure cooker, buddy. >> I have something in mind. I don't want to say anything though. >> No. Do not tell >> I know. I'm not. >> Don't let it out of the bag, but have fun with it. Thank you for your time. Good luck. That's Dylan Thieman, Bears rookie safety here on ESPN 1000 of the Bears Radio Network. >> Jeff Joniak [music] and Tom Thayer chatting about the Bears. It must be Bears Weekly. Well, if it's Bears Weekly, it must be the home of the Bears, [music] >> This segment of Bears Weekly brought to you by Athletico Physical Therapy. Visit athletico.com to request an in-clinic or virtual appointment and start feeling better tomorrow. With Tom Thayer and Jim Miller, I'm Jeff Joniak. Just heard from Dylan Thieman who went to Purdue, then to Oregon. And I think Tom, those stops, as we heard from him, will probably help him adapt considerably quicker as he tries to get to know his teammates in a in a deeper way and try to earn that starting job at safety, whatever position Dennis Allen envisions him playing, probably both posted in the box. >> So, he's been in the Big 10. He's gone to Purdue. He's been a local guy. He's got the surroundings of his family and everything. And now he's got to get on a plane, travel 4 hours out to the West Coast, and he goes to probably a better supporting cast group that he's practiced against every day. He sees a faster brand of football, more ready for his professional career sooner because of the transfer, of the the change of venue, of the different elements that you go through from Purdue to Oregon. So, you know, Dylan talked a lot about his experience, but I think his experience will expedite his ability to be ready to play more immediately at an NFL level. >> Yeah, I I think really for for him, it's going to be more about his in-the-box play that you talked about, Jeff. I mean, there are teams that can go traditional offense. The Bears are one of them. You know, they can go smashmouth football if they need to, heavy personnel. A lot of colleges don't do that. But, he's a quick learner. He's a tough player. He's always around the football, and that's the main thing. He gets a lot of turnovers, and I think that's really what attracted Dennis Allen and why the Bears wanted him a a part of their organization. >> All right. Now, time to listen in to the pride of Lake Zurich, back with the Bears linebacker Jack Sanborn. >> I can feel the energy everywhere. Um I was I still am very close to Chicago with family, friends, and everything like that. So, where to the point where I understood the excitement and everything going around last year, and now um just trying to come and help this team more and um help this team get one or two more extra wins. >> You're here, then you're in Dallas, now you're back here in Chicago. What did you take from your experiences last year that can help you this year? >> Yeah, I mean, I think over there that there are some people, just like in any building, I imagine anywhere in the league and anywhere kind of even outside of football, but you're going to meet some great people and you're going to meet some people that you can really learn a lot from and learn from their experiences and then the experiences that you guys share together and kind of translate that to yourself. And over there, I mean, there are some people over there that are great people that I feel like I learned a lot from and learned a lot and grew grown up a lot and matured a lot and just taking those experiences wherever you go and then bringing them back here and building off of it. >> It seems like the linebackers here at Dennis Allen, he wants the linebackers to be able to play every position. Do you feel that you've developed a little bit more in what you're you can offer a football team in terms of playing multiple spots in this defense? >> Yeah, I mean, I think versatility is always big and I think just mentally getting to that point, especially now. I think this like off-season wise and right now is especially a huge time just learning intricacies of the defense from everywhere and just how your part in that defense fits and kind of in each play and how it works. And just being able to play like you said, all three positions, having that versatility, being dependable, I think it's always huge and it's always an upside. >> What were the nerves like coming out of the opponent's locker room in Soldier Field? >> It was nervous, but also a little bit like exciting in a way, too. Just It was different. I mean, it was like the different side of it and um didn't know really what to expect, but kind of just that day coming back and then, you know, my family in town and everything like that. I do think it'll be one that I'll always remember. >> Well, your family the night before the game, you know, that's a whole added element to it. I'm a local guy, you're a local guy, I played in Chicago, but now you come in and you're part of the opponent and your family's in the visiting hotel. Was was all that a little surreal because you're taking so much into account in a short amount of time? >> It was, but at the same time like I had a lot of time to prepare for it. It's not like I just found out a week ago that oh we're going to Soldier Field. So, definitely able to adjust and understand and be ready for everything. But no, it's I think it was always great to see family. >> Yeah, for sure. For sure. Jack Sanborn our guest here with Tom Thayer, Jeff Joniak. So, this defense is it a a manageable learning experience type defense or is it complicated? >> A little bit of Both. I think with the coaching staff that we got, they make it they really do a great job of teaching and learning and then we can hit the ground running and I think that's the goal and I'm confident in that. >> You got a you got a veteran veteran linebacker coach there of course and Richard Smith. Tell us about him cuz he he he cracks me up when I when I do interview him from time to time. He's a grizzled vet, man. >> Oh, he is. He is for sure and you got to love that. You got to love that old school mentality kind of approach to the game of football and he's got a ton of experience and he's coached a lot of great players, been around a lot of good teams. That's what experience does and so you got to be able to absorb that information that he's given to you and he's a great coach and he he doesn't let us off easy and he's always coaching us. You got to respect that. >> Yeah, now this is interesting because you were a bear but now you're a bear again and you know the whole Dennis Allen you got to do 50 up downs, right? Are you aware of this? >> I I've I've heard of it. >> Can't get past the 50 up downs. >> Yeah, I think we'll figure out [laughter] when that time comes and if I'm told to do my up downs, I'll be doing my up downs with him. >> Yeah. So, what you've learned though just from listening to Dennis Allen talk to about the defense. I I appreciate the old school fiery cuz he's he's a fiery guy. >> Very much like Ben and what you've learned about both in the the minimal time you've been back with these >> They love football and live live for football. So far just great coaches and intense but I I intense in a very good way at the same time. >> want guys like you who love football. That that I don't think if you're if you don't love football, you won't be a Bear. >> Yeah. And I think that's what uh it seems like with them cuz they love it and you get they want you to love it just as much as them and yeah, but both very smart, very knowledgeable of everything that they're doing um and so far I've been loving the chance to get to work with them. >> How how has been the recontact between Ryan Poles and your agent when they came, "Hey, let's call Jack. We got to get him back on this team." >> We weren't 100% sure that like it was going to come with Chicago, but then when Ryan did call, it was kind it was definitely one of those things where not sure I was exactly expecting it. Um but when it did happen and how could I not >> really really think about it, really uh weigh the options and you know, um and I'm no place I'd rather be, right? >> So, my last year I went to the Miami Dolphins, but I always kept an eye on the Chicago Bears because they that was my local home team town and everything. Were you alerted to some of the exciting finishes the Bears had last year? >> Oh, yeah. Um for sure and I think just from here, my girlfriend is a huge Bears fan, family huge Bears fan. So, obviously I've I heard all about it throughout the year last year too, but it's also like even guys like on the team I was and they're from Chicago. Like everybody's got a small little connection to Chicago and the Bears and uh just kind of seeing what the score was wearing stuff like that for sure throughout the weeks. >> Packer Bear rivalry which you grew up with obviously and so close to >> it hasn't slowed down. >> No, slowed down Jack. It has gone it's it's steroid change. I'm telling you it's it's on. >> It's exciting. >> It is and I got to tell you it was the first time in our careers as broadcasters the stadium was actually shaking underneath our feet. >> Oh, yeah. >> And it was Bears And so it was the it was it was so burned in my memory now. I'll never forget the moment. It was almost like a a cinematic moment. >> That's awesome. >> that's kind of the platform from where you guys go now in this rivalry. And of course Ben, he speaks his mind about it. Like this is >> He loves it, I think. >> He really does. >> So it must make you proud though to be a Bear in that vein, right? >> Yeah. And to go beat the Packers. >> Enough said. Jack Sanborn thanks. >> Thank you. >> Appreciate Thanks for having >> Love the finish. Yes, beating the Packers is something of significance for a Chicago-born Bears fan like Sanborn. Multiple position player Tommy with special teams depth piece. It'll be a heck of a competition at that position when you consider a returning De'Mario Jackson, Reuben Hippolyte trying to be a better than he was a year ago. He didn't play a lot, certainly not on defense. Then when he did he got hurt. A rookie Keshawn Elliott is promising. You got Noah Sewell coming off Achilles. His brother Nephi Sewell also in the competition. >> Yeah, you know, and Jack Sanborn he's mentally and physically ready to play all three linebacker positions and contribute on special teams. He's always been a guy that's had a really positive attitude about his professional life and I think that's continues. And you did have that time away that you had an opportunity to learn a little bit more about the National Football League, about you know, different opponents that you prepared or prepared for and different teammates that you prepared with. And so I think all the experiences NFL player has is can be a positive. And for me, I always like Jack Jack's attitude from the moment he got here for the way he carried himself as a Chicago Bear and the attitude he had on his return. So I'm I'm excited to see what he can contribute. In you know, last year training camp Noah Sewell was the guy that really burst onto the scene. We saw a training camp of a really fast guy, dedicated himself into the weight room, and it was evident on his field of play. But, after he recovers from an injury, I think Jack can fill that void immediately while the rest of the guys kind of catch up. >> Yeah, I I don't think uh the Bears ever should have lost him. I think we know that's part of the deal in free agency and what can happen. Uh goes down there with uh Matt Eberflus, and they weren't really good defensively, but he talked about how much he learned and the people he learned from. But, you know, to me Jack is is Here's why the Bears want him back. He's accountable, he's reliable, and he's productive. Uh that's That's the only thing I can say about Jack. Anytime I watched him step on the field, he was making plays. That guy is always around the football. Uh he's well-liked in the locker room, but he just he always seems to be there. He he shows up. He's he's accountable. And why wouldn't uh you know, Dennis Allen really didn't have a a background with him. Uh and so certainly I think he he had a big impact on the Bears organization and why they wanted to resign him and bring him back. >> Hard-nosed and definitely love of the game guy. Exactly what the Bears want. Coming up next, Luke Nieuwmann, a promising interior offensive lineman. Coming up next here on ESPN 1000 with the Bears. >> Welcome back to Bears Weekly on the Bears Radio Network. Here's your host, the [music] voice of the Bears, Jeff Joniak. >> [music] >> Welcome back, everybody, to ESPN 1000 and the Bears Radio Network and Bears Weekly with Tom Thayer and Jim Miller. One of the bright young prospects for the Bears on the offensive line is Luke Nieuwmann. >> I'm feeling great. Uh you know, this offseason I've had a good amount of time to spend around here. You know, I trained with uh you know, a gym in the city and also trained up here periodically throughout the the spring and the winter, and uh yeah, body feels great. Um you know, no issues to complain. You know, I feel strong out there out in OTAs. Uh I feel like there's been, you know, a big difference in terms of my play strength. Um and I I think it's going to really show uh you know, show up in a big way come training camp. >> Now, I want people listening because some, you know, wonder what a workout for a an NFL player looks like, right? It's not 2-hour stay at the gym. It's in the off season, it's a full day of stuff, right? So, give me an example of a of a of a a really good day for Luke Newman when it's just you and and the weights and, you know, getting ready to get ready for the season. >> Sure. So, uh certainly over the last couple years, I spent more time, you know, warming up, getting ready to do the actual lift, you know, uh it's it's crazy how much can change in just a few years from from high school to, you know, being in the pros where you got to take more into account on how to prepare yourself, but, you know, when it comes to the actual weightlifting itself, um you know, if we're working on a squat day, we usually do one compound lift being that squat, uh hit that for a couple sets, you know, in the off season I'd I'd typically go pretty not too heavy, but uh right around the 400, 450 range, and working a lot on tempo, um you know, working a lot of eccentric, um especially with my trainer in the city, you know, whether that be 3 seconds down, one pause, 1 second up, um doing a lot of that, and uh it's kind of supplemented throughout the day with um a lot more hamstring uh strength stuff, so do a lot of um do a lot of hamstring curls, uh do a lot of good mornings, RDLs, um and usually find something else to complement that, you know, working with your quads as well, whether that be some yeah, some split squats as well. Max Brazmer started a couple of games for him. Carson Wentz started five games for him. So there was just inconsistency that really rippled throughout the rest of the offense. And that inconsistency was only exacerbated by watching Sam Darnold do what he did in Seattle and taking them to a Super Bowl. So that was the biggest storyline throughout the season for the Vikings. And I mentioned how it rippled out throughout the rest of the offense. Justin Jefferson had his worst NFL season, and that's including the 2023 season in which he only played 10 games. He had fewer yards last year in which he played 17 games. He had 1,074 or 148 yards and he had 174 yards in 2023 when he missed seven games due to injury. Let that sink in. That is kind of the level that we're talking about when it comes to the Vikings offense, which we're used to seeing be very prolific. It just was not last year. The running game, Jordan Mason, uh, and Aaron Jones kind of a two-headed monster there. Jordan Mason actually outgained Aaron Jones despite only starting five games to Aaron Jones's 12. So they finished 28th in total offense. They finished 26th in scoring offense, 20.2 points per game. So that was the Vikings. Offensively, defensively, they kind of continued to be what they always have been. Brian Flores is a foot on the gas pedal type of defensive coordinator and they blitzed at the highest rate in the league. They had a lot of linebackers involved. Harrison Smith at safety still involved, Byron Murphy at corner. So they had a really good defensive season. They were third in uh total yards allowed. They were, I believe, seventh in points per game allowed, 19.6 points per game. Uh and then they were minus nine in the turnover differential, but that's not because their defense wasn't producing them. It's because they turned the ball over 30 times more than any other team in the league. So, that's a little bit of a recap of where they were last season. The offseason narrative, I'll make this quick. It's the quarterback, right? Like that has driven, I think, a ton of what Minnesota has done. They did also fire their general manager, Adafo Mensah, and kind of went throughout this offseason and free agency and the draft with an interim GM. Uh, so that was that was kind of interesting. They loaded up in the draft on defense. We'll get to that in a little bit, but re really it's this team feels like a team at a crossroads where this time last year we weren't saying that at all. We were talking about the Vikings as a contender in the NFC, if not the entire NFL. And so that is what's so fascinating to me because on the one hand, I could see this team bouncing back if they can get the quarterback play correct in one of the the toughest divisions and be right there with the Lions and be right there with the Packers and the Bears and and kind of compete in the NFC. I could also see us being a year away from the other conversation happening and you kind of being like, "All right, well, what is the future of the Vikings team looking like?" So that's really where I feel like they are right now personally. um their biggest departure this off seasonason and this one is a little bit of an asterisk I will say realistically it's it's kind of a combo with their defensive tackles Jonathan Allen and Javon Hargrave uh they had three and a half sacks each last year they combined for 11 tackles for a loss and just anytime you're kind of losing a duo there on the interior um I think it's significant and that was kind of the Jaylen Naylor offensively uh was kind of a loss for them at wide receiver but really the asterisk part of this is Harrison Smith. 15-year veteran, has been kind of the heartbeat of this Minnesota Vikings defense for such a long time. A lot of people are out there saying that he may have played his last down in the NFL. Um, he is not signed by the Vikings currently. A lot of Vikings people in their building have said publicly, you know, they would welcome him back if he decides to come back, but I think he is very seriously weighing retirement. So, that would be their biggest departure this off seasonason if he indeed does not play again. biggest uh addition. Again, I can make this quick. It's Kyler Murray. Uh they they kind of did the the Tua deal, right? Getting Kyler Murray on a one-year deal that's very very cost-effective uh for their financial balance sheet. And he's coming in to compete with JJ McCarthy. We'll see how that competition plays out in training camp. A lot like the the one we've got here in Atlanta. A lot of people are going to be watching that to to see because again, the pieces are kind of there offensively. It's really just the question of who's going to be running the show, which is why Kyler Murray, you know, if you look at the amount paid, he's not going to be at the top of the list, but for all intents and purposes, he's absolutely the most important uh addition that they have had this offseason. That being said, I love their draft class. Uh when I was going back through it, a lot of guys that I was I was circling ahead of the draft. Caleb Banks, first round pick, defensive tackle, broken foot, seems like he'll be ready for training camp. Uh, I'm always iffy with foot injuries, but he was somebody we talked about early on out of Florida. Could maybe be a fit here in Atlanta. He's a disruptor. Jake Gold was kind of like a guy that I was circling all the way up until the end out of Cincinnati. A rangy linebacker reminds me a lot of Troy Anderson. Uh, so I like him. Dominique Orange, big citrus as Dave Archer liked to call him in the third round. So they really loaded up their defensive line and the spine of their defense there. Finally, what is their team identity and how does it match up with the Falcons? Right now, the thing we know the most about with Minnesota is their defense. I feel very confident that the identity that Brian Flores has put into place there is going to hold. It's going to remain the same. Yes, there's some old faces who may be gone. There's some new faces coming in, but by and large, the identity is going to be there. So I kind of just right now as I'm envisioning it I I believe last year it was 22 to6 Atlanta won but it was it was kind of like for as much as Atlanta's defense dominated in that game it felt like these ones tend to get like a a weird slugfesty type of just like choppy rocky hard gritty type of game which is a little bit different than the Vikings Falcons games from maybe 5 10 years ago where it felt like they were all 38 32 two. I kind of see this one being a little bit defensive heavy. You got the two most blitz happy defensive coordinators in the league last season going toe-to-toe. Both offenses are entering training camp with train with quarterback questions. So, right now, I would have to say that this is going to be kind of like a fun defensive matchup even though there are the pieces on the offensive side of the ball for both teams to turn it into a really really fun uh high-scoring event. So, that is Know Your Foe on the Minnesota Vikings. Again, a reminder, Falcons Audible will be back on Tuesday to kind of preview training camp as we look forward to getting that thing kicked off next week. And then we will be back with our first kind of training camp show on Monday following the first 4 day block of action. [music] So, thank you guys so much for listening to today's episode. I know it was a long one. Thank you so much. Um, and we will see you all next time.

title: Jacoby Brissett | Training Camp 7.26.26 | AZ Cardinals
text: Kobe how does it feel to get that deal done? >> Uh I felt good to be back out there. Uh you know, obviously just standing around wasn't uh particularly fun, but uh you know, it was a good first day. >> You did look pretty sharp considering you haven't had a lot of 11-on-11 work for a while. Like, did you feel sharp when you were doing stuff? >> Uh I mean, my head is like still like spinning right now. Uh but, I was just trying to call the right play and and know what I'm supposed to do to be able to help the other guys. So, uh I got to watch the film to be able to tell you, you know, how I felt. And my head is still all over the place right now. >> Is it a relief to have this done? Is it a weight off your shoulders? >> Oh, for sure. I'm pretty sure I'll probably sleep more than 3 hours tonight. Um and and uh yeah, so and we got an off day tomorrow, so I'll sleep in a little bit. >> I know you joke about, you know, only getting 3 hours of sleep, but was there a point where it did become stressful for you? >> Oh, yes, cuz it's it's it's your livelihood, you know, it's it's it's business. It's it's uh part of this game and uh you know, and being here, obviously wanted to be out there with the guys and and uh that causes another stressor. Uh but, uh you know, just glad it's over with and moving forward. >> How nice was it, you know, some of the guys like Buddha put out a statement, you know, on on Twitter and everything and it seemed like the guys were really supporting you through this. >> me? >> Huh? >> Was that for me? >> Yeah. >> Oh, I'm sitting on the edge. >> [laughter] >> Uh no, it's good. I mean, it it I think that's the the you know, the ultimate um you know, reward in this game is your respect for your teammates. You know, I think that's the I I don't even know if reward is more so the currency is is the the the the respect and the uh recognition from your teammates. I think that's what I mean, I kind of pride myself on it and really that's the only thing I really value. Uh you know, contracts come and go, but you know, your teammates and and the people that you go to work with and the ones that want to go to bat for you, I think that's what uh matters the most. >> Did it feel by yourself or there ever times throughout the off season or maybe early in camp where it might have felt more challenging of how much you participate or wherever you are with negotiations? >> Uh I mean I I I've never had an agent, so I kind of done all of them on my own. Uh I won't say on my own. I have a team that I don't want to make it seem like I'm like a person that does it by myself. Uh but it it it definitely it definitely got dark uh couple times, but uh you know, just just trusting myself to be able to still get up and go to work and go train and things of that nature and and uh you know, I mean, I wasn't here, but I still had ears here. Like I still was uh talking to some guys here, so uh it made me feel a little bit more included. Uh but uh yeah. >> Like Flores talked often times about your experience and and through this process the contract is the one thing, but you eventually learning the offense he wasn't worried about because you are so experienced and because you have so seen so many things. Obviously, there's going to be a certain amount of learning curve, but do you have that same kind of confidence in yourself that ultimately it's different than if a guy had been in the year league one year and missed all that? >> Yeah, I think that's what gave me even more confidence is in myself is knowing that I've been through so many different phases of this thing of football that, you know, I knew once the business got handled, you know, I mean, now the the football is the football and I know I'm you know, take care of that, you know, and I had no uh you know, doubt that you know, I'm I'm going to put the work in, you know, I mean, like I think that's what the reason why we did get a deal done cuz they knew I would get the work done, you know, and uh I think my teammates understood that and obviously coach Flores doesn't know me as well, but uh somebody told him that I would do the work, so >> You obviously came back during mandatory mini camp and didn't start. Sorry. >> You grew your hair out a little bit. >> For now, we'll see. Um you threw me off. You obviously came back during mandatory mini camp and we're we're in meetings at that point. Um do you feel like you're kind of fully up to speed with with learning the offense or is that still a progression? >> Oh, hell no. I'm I'm I think we just ran all day one plays out there for me today. Uh, so I got I got a long way to go, but again, like I said, I mean I'm willing to put the work in. Obviously, um, you know, after this night of sleep that I do get, I'll go back to 3 hours of sleep for work purposes now. Uh, but uh, you know, it is but it's training camp. We're all learning. It's first time in this offense. So, uh, I'm not naive to understand that there's still a lot of work to be done. >> What's been your impression of Mike and just how he operates? >> Uh, it's been good. Uh, you know, obviously, not as much as in person as normally I would have during training camp, but it's been good. Have been able to talk to him on the phone and hear a lot of stories from the guys from OTAs and stuff like that. And then, obviously, being here in training camp and seeing his energy. Um, you know, I think I think it's what, 3 or 4 days I've been here and it's been good. Me and him have had good dialogue and conversations and then, um, yeah. >> Are you able to elaborate a little bit about this off season and when you potentially heard from the team that you would be the starter for this year? Has that been conveyed to you? >> Uh, I mean I think I got to go out there and prove it, you know? I mean, I don't think that's I don't think it's a I mean, it's a a given just because a deal gets done. I think, you know, you go out there and put your best foot forward. I think at the end of the day, no matter what, who money wise, I think as the coach and as the people of the organization, they got to put the best person forward. >> Representing yourself, what was the process of kind of deciding that you wanted to do this holdout and that you wanted to kind of push for more money rather than just, you know, showing up and and playing on the previous deal? >> I think that's the business of this this league. >> How did you come to that decision? >> I think it I think it kind of just unfolds as it as the business side goes, you know? >> You said that you said that at times it got dark for you and just in general, like, was there ever a fear that this might not happen or was it more so a matter of just when it will it happen? >> Uh, I think a mixture of both. I think you have that. Uh, you know, nothing is guaranteed. Nothing is given in this league. So, uh, you know, you you you wake up just like the football aspect of getting up and one day at a time you do the same thing with the business side of it and and um, you know, you're you're you're honest with the the people that you're, you know, uh, conversating with it and I think it's just obviously knowing who you are as a person, as a player and and um, I will say it's confidence but just having the I think the respect for yourself. Uh, you know, I think plays a big part in it. >> Are you surprised at how long the whole process took and are you pleased with the end results? >> Oh, yeah. I mean, I'm ready to go out and play. You know what I mean? I'm my my like I said, my mind's racing, my heart's racing to still too. Uh, uh, but I mean, with these things is never a timetable, you know? It's just a matter of when, you know, whether some happens or it doesn't happen, you know? And um, you know, glad it's over with and and now it's it was onward. >> You put up pretty decent numbers last year. Where do you need to be better this year going into this season? >> Uh, I think everything. I think you I I think you you always have to get better at everything. The things that you do good, you got to do those better. Things you do bad, you got to find a way to get those better. So, I think uh, I think it's a matter of everything. >> Do you think you can benefit from, you know, last year obviously the first five games Kyler started and then you kind of had to take over and there was a whole situation with all that and then you can benefit from this is your team potentially, you know, if you're the number one, the starter and everything that you can start fresh and from the beginning? >> Uh, say that again. >> Sorry, I kind of rambled. >> Yeah, a little bit. >> Anyway, do you think there's any benefit then instead of coming in in the middle of the season as a starter that maybe starting from week one that you can kind of build the season? >> Um, yes and no. It's a different system. It's It's different coaches. It's different season. Um you know, but obviously you rely on past experiences. I mean, I'm just going to my year 11. Uh so, and I've been in so many different roles throughout my career that um I think you you don't just bank on the last year, but you bank on the the previous years as well. Uh and I think it the the thing that stayed consistent is you got to go work and you got to, you know, put the time in. >> Jacoby, a lot of people would say that winning is not a quarterback stat, but how frustrating was it last year for you knowing you're out there 12 games and you go 1 and 11 in those starts? How tough is that? >> Yeah, it's tough. I mean, we're not going out there to lose. Uh so, you go out there and you try to put your best foot forward and and and uh >> What would you say to the people that might be skeptical of of your holdout given the record last year? >> Skeptical about what? >> The fact that holding out after going 1 and 11 for a team that struggled a year ago. >> So, what's the question? >> What would you say to those folks? >> I could care less. Deal got done. >> Jacoby, what was the moment like when you walked into the locker room and the deal was done? Were there hugs? Were there high-fives? Just what was that moment like? >> Yeah, we had cake. No, it was it was good. Uh just the the like I said, the the currency is the respect of your teammates, you know, and the people that you go to work with. Obviously, some of these guys here don't know me from you know, uh from last year, but a lot of guys that were uh here with me last year and and been able to, you know, come up to me and and obviously um their excitement for me. Uh you know, I think that I think that meant meant more to me than the than the actual contract getting done, to be honest with you. >> Getting together with the guys in Florida, how beneficial is that just keeping that connection? >> Uh it was good. Um you know, I hadn't seen them in 5 6 months, you know, so you know, I think it was more so just to like spend time with each other um and, you know, hang out. We threw a little bit. Uh You obviously didn't see the other stuff that we were doing, but play golf, play basketball, you know, just things like that just to be around each other. >> Can you give me a rundown of the hole-in-one? >> Oh, I mean, excuse me. Uh I had a terrible shot and it went in and sometimes you you're so good that you get lucky, you know? >> Okay, when you scroll through the playbook, um the Mike LaFleur playbook, um are there any concepts that stand out as like, "Ooh, I can't wait to to run this type of concept?" Or have you you know, in your experience seen pretty much everything in there, at least uh conceptually? >> Uh have I seen everything? I I don't know if I've seen everything, but uh you know, a lot of a lot of familiarity uh with a lot of things that we did last year. Obviously, um different wrinkles and things of that nature, getting into it different ways. Uh you know, I'm I'm I'm just excited to get good with the guys and I don't care if it's taking a knee 20 times, you know what I mean? I'm just get I'm ready to get in the huddle and and, you know, just be with the guys. >> I guess that you guys met the first time at the Senior Bowl, I guess 11 years >> Yeah, 11 years ago. >> has your relationship been with him since that time, if anything, and what are the early impressions working with him? >> Yeah, I think it's it's been a a mutual respect after the Senior Bowl and having that I think we spent like a week in Mobile together and uh you know, when obviously when seeing him on other teams and things of that nature. Uh you know, obviously going up to each other and literally the first time every time we go up to each other is, "I remember you from the Senior Bowl." Even though we've already said it already, you know? So, it's things like that and actually saw him at the Four Seasons in uh on vacation 2 years ago. So, it's funny that I see him now, but uh it's been good. It's it's again, like I haven't been around a lot of these guys for a while, so it's all it's all kind of new and fresh and and building that relationship. Um you know, I'm not going to sit up here and say that we're best friends because that'll be a lie, you know what I mean? But I think you for one you have the respect for the person, but then it starts to build as far as the the relationship. >> You already have a rapport with Trey McBride, Marvin Harrison Jr., Michael Wilson. What's been your early impressions of guys like Jeremiah Owusu-Koramoah? >> well, I I played with KB in New England and obviously I haven't went with Jeremiah yet, but obviously getting it being able to be here and watch him you know, practice and and do his thing. Obviously I see why we paid him $50 million. That's for sure. >> Thanks, Jacoby.

title: LB Mack Wilson Sr. | Training Camp 7.26.26 | AZ Cardinals
text: You tweeted rocket ship with like excitement for Jacoby. I guess what are your thoughts? He's been here but to officially have him here for this year. >> Yeah, I mean it's a super dope honestly. You know, obviously when Jacoby first came here I got a chance to, you know, really get to know the person and that just told me everything I needed to know on what type of player he was going to be. And he's been nothing but great since he walked, you know, stepped foot in that building and I feel like, you know, his his future is ahead of him and can't wait to see, you know, how successful he'll be this season. >> How do you guys players balance you wanting him to get his but also be there, be on the field, get the team ready for the season? Like how do you kind of >> I mean at the end of the day, you know, people have their own stuff going on and you know, we stand behind our teammates on whatever they believe and I'm never going to question a guy uh to, you know, do what he supposed to do, you know, for himself and his family and things like that. All we can do is support him no matter what he do in life, you know, I feel like Jacoby handled it well and he got it done at the end of the day. So, we're excited as a team and you know, we're ready to move forward. >> When you look back last year at what you guys did as a defense and obviously you missed a big chunk of the year and a lot of guys missed big chunks. Um does it boil down to that that you guys just didn't have the players that you needed to have out there? Is there other stuff you want to see get better? >> Yeah, I mean it's always next man up mentality and you know, obviously we, you know, want the guys behind us the twos and the threes to like they going to play every Sunday because obviously things happen and you know, last season was a test of that. We lost a lot of guys and you know, we weren't able to hold up defensively down the line I feel like and you know, it definitely plays a big part when you don't have your leaders out there your signal caller out there and things like that. So, yeah, I will say that. >> You mentioned that and Cody was one of the guys that stepped in your place. Now it seems like you two are sharing the field a lot more than you did previously. What have you learned about him as a player now that the two of you are sharing that huddle? >> Yeah, he's matured a lot. Honestly, Uh, just seeing him from his first start till now, I I I I love Kibi trying to tell Nick like, "Hey, let me and Cody like switch positions sometimes just to let him get some Mike run. I want to go back to Will and rush a little bit and things like that." So, uh, definitely been able to, uh, see him grow in things like that and he's going to make a huge step this year. >> Is it working? >> No, it didn't work. >> He not letting me change. >> [laughter] >> Where is his game kind of progressed, um, you know, from from last, you know, maybe October, November when he first started getting in there to now? >> Just his knowledge of the game and understanding of the playbook, I would say, uh, like I said, Cody can play any linebacker spot on the field. I feel like he's so smart and, um, just being able to to hone in on that is going to be huge because, you know, we got to have that flexibility, obviously. It's a long season, a lot of stuff happen and, uh, just got to be ready to go at all times. >> Matthew, I don't know many people outside this building that believe you guys will win many games this year. How do you guys handle that or do you even worry about the outside noise? >> Yeah, I mean, obviously, we all see it. You know, everybody sees it, you know, but it's something about, you know, this team that I feel like, you know, we so resilient and things like that and, you know, we just got to block out the noise, take it one day at a time because at the end of the day, we know what type of guys we have in the locker room. Uh, we know what type of team we can be and, you know, we just building that foundation right now and once September get here, we just going to start letting the bullets fly. >> I know it's early and you've obviously played against divisional teams quite a bit, but having Mike here now and his experience at LA and San Francisco, are you able to maybe get a better idea of how to defend certain things you might see just from what might be sprinkled into this offense here now? >> Yeah, definitely. Uh, coach Mike super smart, understands the game to a T. Uh, and obviously with him coming from the Rams and, you know, that San Fran tree and things like that, obviously we a lot of the stuff that he's doing, I feel like it's going to transfer to some of those opponents that we'll see in our division. And, um, it'd be dope to see how he stopped the stopped the uh, play sometimes and just break down the blocking scheme and what they looking for and it's just so helpful because obviously we be wanting to know what our offense be looking at when they trying to attack us and things like that. So, him being able to do that it would be so dope to see and it allows us to understand stuff a little bit more as well. >> Great. Thanks, man. >> Real talk.

title: OL Paris Johnson Jr. | Training Camp | AZ Cardinals
text: I think everybody here was was was [snorts] was happy to see that. Obviously, you know, I found it online like everybody else in the hot tub back there. So, it was cool to send it around to the guys who were just trickling in to the locker room. Everybody was hyped that, you know, he's back full-time. >> He said there was a cake. True story? >> There was a cake. >> Yeah. That's what he said. >> I didn't see a cake. I'll find out after this. Jacoby, was there a cake? You got a cake? Who ate the cake? Oh. Yeah, that's crazy. Well, I guess I missed out on the cake. Appreciate you telling me. Now I know. >> What is it about him that everyone seems to gravitate towards? >> Yeah, um again, I think just the I think just the leadership in the huddle that he has as a quarterback. It's something that's a very small thing, but you're able to notice it on on game day. I think it's I think it's the composure. I think that's the point of leadership. I think leadership isn't, "Hey, guys, get in tight. Get in tight." like okay, anybody I can say that, you know, right now. But I think I think it's the composure when we have we make those the big plays last year. And it's the composure when we had the plays that were, you know, um uh that that might have ended the drive early. I think it's that composure, you know, the way he came the way he came off the field and the way he was able to take the field after. You notice that he kept his energy the same. It wasn't ebbs and flows of energy. I feel like he controlled his emotions and the controllables well, and I think guys in the huddle were able to notice that and guys that are on that same kind of wavelength pattern, you know. >> You only should have seen kind of what this offense can do with everybody healthy, him back there, Jeremiah, and everybody together. >> Oh, yeah, it's exciting. I think we have a lot of young talent um here, especially with the addition of Jay Love here having him in the huddle so fun. Um he can't wait to get the ball and hit a spin move or a hurdle. You can tell he's he's itching to do it, you know. We watch like the Indy tape and stuff with the running backs are doing the O unit meetings and you see he's he's ready to hit all his moves like he's in college. So he has a skip to beat and he's still motivated to make all those same plays. So to have him along with Jacoby back full-time um on the field with us and you know, Trey's 99 overall. So you know what you got when you got 99 overall um their guy catching the ball. So I think this will be a fun year. >> Earlier today coach alluded to when the pads come on on Tuesday, that's when the run game starts to to get worked on. He said it was a pad it's been a passing camp since he's been here. So is that like when the pads come on for an offensive lineman, is that kind of like you guys feel complete? Okay, let's go. >> Um yes and no. I will say that personally and you can ask Froholdt Isaac anybody that's been around the league for a little bit. Um I would say that with or without pads, with or without spiders across the league, you know, when it's time to put that hand down, the run game's the same. So I'll say if anything, pads is even it's it's it's it's a lot more fun to play with pads because now we got something to grab. Right now it feels like we're like a high school football camp and the D line is trying to play all slippery. You know what I mean? But with or without pads, we we still have all this mass, we're the same size. So the nice thing is they have those nice handles. So if anything, it just gets even easier. So when you bully somebody in the run game in t-shirts or shorts, it's even easier to do it in pads in my opinion. So but either way like the way we're going to rock off the ball with or without spiders rest of the camp could be spiders, it's going to be the same intensity. Um obviously you got to be more smart in certain combination blocks and stuff not to get guys hurt, that's true. But um there's going to be those certain blocks like when you get to the second level, when you get to the linebacker, obviously I get up to Mac, get up to Cody. I'm not just going to throw my whole body into him with no pads. That's not smart for myself. That's not smart for his health. Obviously, when the pads get on, you know, anybody can get it. DBs, you know, linebackers, you know. If a guy doesn't see me coming and get tackled, then obviously I can really go out of my way to make something happen that would be um a bad teammate right now. So, you have less of those bad teammate plays. But either way, you're rocking off. Yeah, I want to hit somebody without getting in trouble for life. Something that'd be dirty. You don't want to make dirty plays, you know. >> Harris, how nice was it just to get off the pup list and actually like get on the field with the players? >> Oh, yeah. I mean, I was catching a lot of heat from from the O-line, you know, um for being on pup. I told them it was for 48 hours. Um 48-hour pup mission. I was saying to like make them relax. I was like, "I'll literally be back on Saturday for walk-throughs." Um you know, it was all part of the plan. All part of um just making sure that my body is completely whole. Um uh then I felt fine. Um it's just protocol. And um right now I feel even better.
