title: 'It was so full circle': Midge Purce's World Cup experience has her hyped for '27 | WSS Conversation
text: I think what we have been looking for for a very long time is equal investment [music] in a product that has the same amount of value or can gain and and access [music] the same amount of value as a product that has been heavily invested in for triple quadruple decades [music] worth of time. And on the business side, there's just so many signs that this is a great product, women's sports, and I think [music] great products will sell once you get good people selling them. >> This episode of Women's Sports Sunday's conversation is presented by TJ Maxx. >> We're here today with Harvard's own Midge Purce, a two-time NWSL champ, entrepreneur, a podcaster, an equal pay advocate. She does it all, and she's kind enough to take some time [music] to join us here on Women's Sports Sunday. Midge, thank you for being here. >> Thank you for having me. What an introduction. >> Well, you've done some incredible things, and I have to start with the World Cup because I know that you were an ambassador for this year's games, which culminated with the incredible finale between Spain and Argentina. What was it like being the ambassador in the city which the final was happening, getting to represent New York and New Jersey, where you live, where you work on a daily basis with Gotham FC, and getting to see the world transcend for this incredible event that went 5 weeks and allowed us all to become soccer fans? >> I mean, it was unfathomable to me. I had never been to a men's World Cup game ever in my entire life. So, for it to be right here at home, and not just at home in the country, but literally in the backyard. Like, we go to MetLife all the time for concerts, we go to MetLife for football games, and to be there for something as singular as the World Cup was insane. >> What was the final like? Because that was a battle that goes into extra time with Spain pulling off the defeat over Argentina. Seeing the fans, seeing two different countries getting to witness this moment as an ambassador, watching all that take place in the pomp and circumstance, what was that like? >> Honestly, as an ambassador, as a fan of the sport, you know, as someone who's played the game my entire life, I brought my dad. It was so full circle. It was It was a really beautiful moment to be able to experience it and be there. I was just like, this is to date for me the best sporting event to take place cuz I think that's what happens every World Cup final, every time the World Cup comes around. But, maybe more controversial, I didn't think the game was that that good. I was kind of bummed that it wasn't a more exciting game. The the game before, England-France, that was a crazy thriller and given I don't think everyone was really trying their absolute hardest to defend in that game. It still was a bit more entertaining. When you have a side that doesn't put up any shots on frame, that takes a bit away from, you know, the thriller that you're you're really looking for, but regardless, any World Cup final is is an amazing game to be a part of and I I really am super humbled and feel really privileged to have been there. And now that the men's World Cup is over, it's got me thinking that we are less than a year away from the women's World Cup in 2027. So, so back in 2023, I know you weren't able to participate with the United States Women's National team because of your quad injury, but when they exited in the round of 16, you made a pretty bold statement that everyone should be terrified of this squad and what they can accomplish in 2027. So, years removed from that moment, what's your confidence level in this group going forward knowing that the next World Cup is just on the horizon? Yeah, I think in 2023, it was a more inexperienced roster. I think a lot of the stars and players who are veterans that you look to to deliver now were it was their first World Cup then. It was their first big tournament then and I think now even with the leadership of Emma Hayes, you've seen a turn in the identity of that team and I think everyone should be really excited. >> One of the games United States women's national team won in its fight for equal pay was a 50/50 World Cup prize split with both the men's team and the women's teams. What does an increase like that do not just for teams being able to support one another, but also help the women solely focus on soccer? >> That 50/50 split was a statement about value that that we collectively made on the men's and the women's side. That to me was one of the bigger signals globally that look, even if we can't change FIFA, if we can't change, you know, even bigger powers that are outside of our control, we want it to be very very clear that we value these trophies equally in this country and we value these players and their effort and their sweat and their tears and their grind equally and it's just as important. >> As you see new CBAs get negotiated all over the place at WNBA, multiple women's professional sports leagues that continue to pop up, what's your level of optimism with the future for the NWSL and women's sports leagues as a whole that equal pay will be a routine thing across the board? >> Yeah, I think I think it's a little bit different. I don't like it's not as much just equal pay, I think and I think that's where we a lot of people get confused. I think what we have been looking for for a very long time is equal investment in a product that has the same amount of value or can gain and and access the same amount of value as a product that has been heavily invested in for triple, quadruple worth of time. And I'm looking forward to it. I'm extremely optimistic. I think we like on the business side, there's just so many signs that this is a great product, women's sports. And I think great products will sell once you get good people selling them. >> When you came into the NWSL to this point now and seeing more teams pop up in the investment and being able to see your games on nationally televised broadcast, how do you think the investment has increased or where I guess have you seen the investment in in women's soccer here stateside increase the most? >> when I get this question now, I like to zoom really, really narrowly in and just shout out and give so much credit to the Tisch family who bought Gotham FC. I think they are an amazing, exemplary model to look at for what good investment looks like in women's sports. They've come in and they've completely turned our club around. We have a new stadium that we'll be playing in that's, you know, up-to-date and and just worth it being our own. And we have a new facilities that will be completely our own here at Gotham. So, uh I would look to Carolyn and Emily Tisch for that. >> So, you mentioned the new stadium. I know you're moving into the soccer specific stadium in Queens in 2028 along with the New York City FC in in the MLS. What What does that space, having a soccer specific space, do to change the vibe for your home games? >> You know, 2028's a long ways away. >> [laughter] >> Uh or at least in my head it's a long ways away. I think that for the club, it's just an enormous step in making the professionalism of women's soccer in New Jersey, New York, it's really solidifying the professionalism of women's soccer in New Jersey, New York. I think it's uh a really cool step. I think the City Field game that we had showed that there's a lot of people who haven't had access to us who would be super interested in seeing and being a part of this family that we're building. And while we know that it's a bit of an inconvenience to a lot of the fans, the tried and true who have been a part of us, we're going to do our best to keep them around. I think the the club is really excited about everything and the players are really excited and whoever's on that roster at that time, whoever's still at the club or who comes in, I think they'll make it a worthwhile investment. >> in 2023, you were the championship MVP in leading Gotham to a title. In the first game of 2024, you suffered a season-ending injury and you missed the Olympics. You make it back for 2025, you help your team to another trophy. How did you balance the highs and the lows that it took to be able to get back to that place where you were competing at a high level? >> Yeah, I mean, I think that's just sports. I can go around the locker room and I can walk you through a really tumultuous and just volatile story for each and every player who's on that roster. And part of being professional athlete is figuring out how to be resilient and how how to bounce back and control your controllables and be the best possible version of yourself that you can be at any given time and that's not always you know, playing in a championship and healthy and doing all the amazing things you do on the field. Best, sometimes that is recovering from an ACL or just trying to get back and >> and and have reaction times that aren't that don't resemble a child. >> What was the hardest part of the recovery process for you mentally or physically? >> I think the hardest part mentally was expecting my physicality to come back quicker than it did. Uh the off-the-field piece was was pretty seamless when I wasn't able to play. Um and even just the, uh, return to play protocols of just getting back into the games and stuff was wasn't too hard, but it was, you know, when I actually got out on the field, I would try to react to things and I would try to move a certain way and my body was wouldn't be intact with my mind. I would be like, "Go, we're going left." But my feet would still be on the ground and that's a really surreal experience that I I just had never It had never even dawned on me that this is how people can feel. Um, and that took way longer than I expected to to get to get right. >> I can only imagine. I mean, just the mental battle where your body's telling you one thing and your mind is doing another and vice versa, but in that time that you were working to working your way back onto the field, I know that you were able to get a couple looks off, Paris Fashion Week, New York Fashion Week, and then you rock the runway at the Sports Illustrated Swimsuit Show. How have you found your style and broken into the world of fashion? >> Tobin Heath gave me my first pair of Jordans back in Portland. She gave me a pair of threes. Uh, I think they were concretes. Uh, and that's kind of how I got into the Jordan world and then from kind of the shoe game, I started just exploring more and more things that I like and how I like to look. There are certain silhouettes that I think I'm super just partial to cuz I like certain shapes, but just meeting people and being in New York and, uh, really being open to being comfortable with what I like, not necessarily what everyone else likes. I think my style isn't always mainstream and then sometimes it is really mainstream. So, it really is just the, I think the confidence to be comfortable with whatever it is that you feel good in. >> Do you style all of your own looks for games? >> For games, for sure. I actually, I haven't done a true game day fit in quite some time. I used to do them a few years ago. I think even maybe the first year we got the name Gotham, but since then I I kind of sneak into the >> into the locker room with a hat and some sweatpants. So, I definitely dress myself these days. >> So, outside of fashion, you are the queen of side quests. You made your Broadway debut. In Chicago, you produced a reality show. You have your own podcast. Of all the stuff that you fill your off time with, which doesn't seem like you have much time considering how much you do, like what's the most impactful or the one that you feel like yourself the most in? >> I think the most impactful just venture that I've ever done would have been founding the Black Women's Player Collective, for sure. When I would go to those events and when I was the executive director for, I think, one or two years, those events were just so heartwarming and it was amazing to see so many players throughout the league come together to be a part of something so much bigger than sport and give back in a way that really touched the hearts and lives of a lot of kids. Uh I'm working on something else to give back uh cuz I do think that it is, you know, every person's responsibility that we are gifted with something special to return to the world in some way that only we can. So, I'm excited to uh come out with that soon. >> How has being on the other side of interviews like this one on your podcast, Confessions of an Elite Athlete, changed your perspective on the role the media plays? >> I think something that's really unique about Confessions of an Elite Athlete, and this is why when I originally wrote the show, I didn't want to be the host. I was looking for someone else to be the talent on it and I just wanted to EP the podcast, but part of what makes it so special is that there are some questions and some realities that only another athlete can really speak to and understand. It's almost like you're speaking your own language when you're talking to people. So, I think that's something that separates the podcast from I think general media is that sometimes we get into conversations that normal media wouldn't actually ask. Um and that's part of what makes it unique. >> How long does it take you to get someone to truly open up? Because I know that a podcast format allows for a more nuanced conversation and some of the things that people say on your show peel back a curtain and layers that we might not have expected to get to. How quickly do you feel like you can get to the core of someone's story? >> You know, it varies. It varies on how good I am at my job that day. Sometimes I'm not very good >> and I don't make people feel comfortable enough to tell me things that they don't want to talk about and sometimes I have the right energy and and people want to share with me. Um but I it just it just depends. Depends on my relationship with the person, you know, I had a really you know, amazing conversation with Ali Krieger the other day and I well, I shouldn't have released that. You can tell I'm I adore Ali and I can't wait for her episode to come out and she's just such a phenomenal human being and we had just easily one of my favorite conversations ever. Um but I know Ali. We we walked in Sports Illustrated swim together and that works better than, you know, maybe a Todd Gurley who I see at Super Bowl and I'm like, "Hey, will you come to my podcast?" Uh so it just depends on the relationships. There's a lot of factors, but um I'm doing my best. >> Well, you're doing a great job and I want to bring us home now because you're in the middle of a season. What is it going to take for Gotham to go back-to-back this year? >> Oh. I you know, we got a lot of great pieces. Uh the other day we for the first time came back I think in club history from a 2-0 deficit and I can't tell you what the feeling was looking over and seeing Sam Kerr and Denise O'Sullivan come off the bench at a time like that. I mean, our roster is just so deep and so talented and we're still figuring out, you know, relationships and how to play well together. So I think it's going to take every single person on this roster and it's it's going to be a really special year. >> Oh, we're wishing you the absolute best of the best this fall. Congratulations on all the things you have accomplished, all of the many things that make up Midge Purce on and off the field and we appreciate you spending some time with us here today. Thanks so much. >> Thank you for having me. conversation is presented by T.J. Maxx. Never uniform, always you.
